unit-ww501.title: Wordly Wise · Lesson 1
unit-ww501.source: Wordly Wise 3000 Book 5, Lesson 1 (photos in Drive)

summary.text: The fifteen words of Wordly Wise 3000 Book 5, Lesson 1: accustom, alert, assign, budge, burly, companion, compatible, concept, distract, jostle, obedient, obstacle, patient, pedestrian, and retire — including the extra forms the book teaches (accustomed, assignment, distraction, obedience, patience, retirement) and the words that carry more than one meaning.

why.text: These fifteen words show up everywhere once you own them — and vocabulary is the one part of English where a few minutes of practice, spread across days, beats an hour of cramming every time. The tricky ones here are the shape-shifters: alert, patient and retire each mean different things in different sentences.

objectives.text: Give the meaning of all fifteen Lesson 1 words when they appear in a brand-new sentence.
Tell the multiple meanings apart: alert as a warning vs. wide-awake, patient as a person vs. willing to wait, retire as stopping work vs. going to bed.
Use the related forms — assignment, distraction, obedience, patience, retirement — as comfortably as the base words.

nextUp.text: Cards first, once through. Then a quiz round a day beats one long session.

cards.def:
**To make familiar — to get someone used to something.** (verb)
• accustomed (adj.): usual ("our accustomed places") or used to ("accustomed to the dark").
cards.hint: Think 'custom' hiding inside — what you're used to becomes your custom.

cards.def:
**Watchful; wide-awake.** (adjective)
• As a verb: to warn to be ready — "the sign alerted drivers."
• As a noun: the warning itself — "a fire alert."
cards.hint: One word, three jobs: being watchful, warning someone, or the warning itself.

cards.def:
**To pick someone for a job, or give out work to be done.** (verb)
• assignment (n.): the work that got given out.
• A coach assigns positions; a teacher assigns homework.
cards.hint: A-S-S-I-G-N: someone in charge signs you up for it.

cards.def:
**To move or shift — usually just barely, or not at all.** (verb)
• Almost always shows up with 'wouldn't' or 'couldn't': the trunk wouldn't budge.
cards.hint: If it budges, it barely moved. If it won't, it's going nowhere.

cards.def:
**Big and strongly built.** (adjective)
• Describes bodies, not personalities — a burly mover, a burly linebacker.
cards.hint: Burly rhymes with 'surely' — surely you don't want to arm-wrestle him.

cards.def:
**Someone who spends time with you or does things with you.** (noun)
• A travel companion, a walking companion — company, in person form.
cards.hint: Same root as 'company' — the person keeping you company.

cards.def:
**Getting along well together.** (adjective)
• People can be compatible; so can roommates, teammates, even chargers and phones.
cards.hint: Com- = together. Compatible things fit together without a fight.

cards.def:
**A general idea or thought about something.** (noun)
• The concept comes first; the details come after — "we started with the concept of helping our community."
cards.hint: A concept is the idea before it grows details.

cards.def:
**To pull someone's thoughts or attention away from what they're doing.** (verb)
• distraction (n.): the thing doing the pulling — sirens, pop-ups, a buzzing phone.

**To push or shove.** (verb)
• Crowd word: you get jostled in packed hallways, stadiums, subways.
cards.hint: Sounds like 'hustle and jostle' — elbows in a crowd.

cards.def:
**Doing what one is asked or told.** (adjective)
• obedience (n.): the state of doing what you're told — what puppy school teaches.
cards.hint: OBEY is hiding right at the front of it.

cards.def:
**Something that blocks you from moving forward.** (noun)
• A fallen tree on the trail, a wall in your way — or something invisible, like stage fright.
cards.hint: An obstacle stands in the way — that's its whole job.

cards.def:
**Willing to wait without complaining.** (adjective)
• As a noun: a person in a doctor's care.
• patience (n.): the willingness to wait — the thing long lines test.
cards.hint: The waiting-room joke is real: patients need patience.

cards.def:
**A person who is walking; someone traveling on foot.** (noun)
• Crosswalks, sidewalks and walk signals all exist for pedestrians.
cards.hint: Ped- = foot (like pedal). A pedestrian runs on foot power.

cards.def:
**To stop working for good, usually because of age.** (verb)
• Second meaning: to go to bed — "I retired early."
• retirement (n.): the years of no longer working.
cards.hint: Both meanings are about stopping for a rest — one for a night, one for good.

questions.q: After a week at the cabin, Mara had grown ___ to the rooster crowing at dawn — she slept right through it.
steps: Find the clue: she now sleeps through a noise that used to wake her — she is USED TO it.
Match to the list: accustomed means used to; that is the fit.
Check the impostors: obedient is about following orders, burly is about build, compatible is about getting along — none mean 'used to'.

ex.main: **Accustomed.** The sentence describes getting used to something over time — accustom's whole job.
ex.tip: On fill-in-the-blank vocab, find what the sentence PROVES happened first, then pick the word that means that.

questions.q: In which sentence is 'alert' used as a NOUN?
opts: The alert crossing guard spotted the runaway cart.
The weather service issued a flood alert for the valley.
Loudspeakers alerted swimmers to leave the water.
Stay alert during the last five minutes of the game.
questions.hint: The noun is the warning itself — a thing you can issue.
steps: Recall alert's three jobs: adjective (watchful), verb (to warn), noun (the warning signal).
Test each sentence: 'alert crossing guard' describes the guard — adjective. 'Loudspeakers alerted' is an action — verb. 'Stay alert' describes you — adjective.
'Issued a flood alert' — the alert is a THING being issued. That is the noun.

ex.main: **'Issued a flood alert.'** If you can put 'a' or 'the' in front of it and it names a thing, it is the noun.
ex.tip: Wordly Wise loves part-of-speech questions on multi-meaning words. Ask: is it describing, doing, or naming?

questions.q: The drama teacher will assign the parts for the play on Friday. What does 'assign' mean here?
questions.hint: Who decides which student plays which role?
steps: The teacher is deciding who gets which part — matching people to positions.
That is assign's first meaning: to select for a position.
Its cousin meaning — giving out work, like homework — uses the same idea: someone in charge hands out who-does-what.

ex.main: **To select people for positions.** Casting a play is assigning at its purest: one person in charge, matching people to roles.
ex.tip: Assign has two flavors — assigning PEOPLE to spots, and assigning WORK to people. Both start with someone in charge.

questions.q: The puppy planted all four paws, and no amount of leash-pulling would make him ___.
steps: Picture it: something refusing to move even a little.
Budge means to move or shift — and it almost always appears with 'wouldn't' or 'couldn't'.
Jostle is pushing THROUGH a crowd, distract is about attention, retire is about stopping work — only budge is about the not-moving itself.

ex.main: **Budge.** 'Wouldn't budge' is practically one word in English — refusal to move even slightly.
ex.tip: Some vocabulary words live inside set phrases. Budge nearly always travels with a 'not'.

questions.q: Which person is best described as 'burly'?
questions.hint: Big AND strongly built — both parts have to be true.
steps: Burly = big and strongly built, so check each person against BOTH parts.
Wiry means thin and springy — strong maybe, big no. Tall-and-thin fails the strongly-built half. A toddler fails the big half.
The broad-shouldered firefighter is the only one who is both.

ex.main: **The big, broad-shouldered firefighter.** Burly is a two-part word: size plus strength. Half credit does not count.
ex.tip: When a definition has an AND in it, wrong answers usually satisfy exactly one half.

opts: Someone who spends time or does things with you
steps: Companion comes from the same root as company — someone keeping you company.
The key is WITH: a companion does things alongside you.
A neighbor merely lives nearby, a rival competes against you, a boss directs you — none of those require the together part.

ex.main: **Someone who spends time or does things with you.** The with is the whole word.
ex.tip: Root families are free hints: companion, company, accompany — all about being together.

opts: Two magnets pushing away from each other
Two apps that crash whenever both are open
A cat and the neighbor's dog that chases it daily
Lab partners who finish each other's ideas without arguing
questions.hint: Compatible things work well side by side.
steps: Compatible means getting along well together — no friction.
Scan for friction: repelling magnets, a chase, crashing apps — all three are conflict in costume.
The lab partners who work smoothly together are the only friction-free pair.

ex.main: **The lab partners.** Every other option is a picture of things clashing — which is the exact opposite, incompatible.
ex.tip: For 'which pair fits the word' questions, hunt for the conflict. The odd one out is usually your answer.

questions.q: "Our science fair project began with a simple ___: what if plants could water themselves?" Which word fits?
questions.hint: The idea comes first; the project grows from it.
steps: The blank names the starting IDEA behind the project.
Concept means exactly that — a general idea or thought that things get built from.
An obstacle would block the project, a distraction would derail it, a companion would just watch.

ex.main: **Concept.** Projects, inventions and stories all start as concepts — the idea before the details arrive.
ex.tip: 'Began with' and 'started from' are concept's favorite neighbors in a sentence.

questions.q: Which one is a 'distraction' while you are doing homework?
opts: A sharpened pencil on the desk
A phone buzzing with game invites
questions.hint: Which one pulls your attention off the homework?
steps: A distraction is something that PULLS your thoughts away from the task.
Test each item: pencil, water and a finished worksheet all sit quietly — no pull.
The buzzing phone actively grabs your attention away. That is the distraction.

ex.main: **The buzzing phone.** A distraction has to do something — it pulls. Objects that just sit there are scenery.
ex.tip: Distract literally means 'pull away from the track'. Look for the thing doing the pulling.

questions.q: Coming off the crowded bus, Theo was ___ so hard he nearly dropped his backpack.
questions.hint: Crowds do this with their elbows.
steps: The scene is a crowd plus a shove hard enough to knock something loose.
Jostle means to push or shove — the crowd word exactly.
Assigned, accustomed and retired have nothing to do with pushing.

ex.main: **Jostled.** Crowded bus + nearly dropped backpack = shoved. Jostle is the push-and-shove of packed places.
ex.tip: Jostle almost always comes with a crowd attached. See a crowd in the sentence, check for jostle in the options.

questions.q: Which action shows a dog being 'obedient'?
questions.hint: Obedient = doing what one is TOLD.
steps: Obedient means doing what one is asked or told — so look for a command being followed.
Only one option contains a command at all: 'sit'.
The dog sits when told — asked, then done. That is obedience; the rest are just dog moments.

ex.main: **Sitting on 'sit'.** Obedience needs two parts: an instruction, and someone following it. No command, no obedience — just behavior.
ex.tip: For obedient/obedience questions, first find the order being given. No order in the sentence is usually a wrong answer.

questions.q: The runners rounded the corner and found their path blocked by a fallen branch. In this sentence, the branch is:
questions.hint: What do you call a thing standing in the way?
steps: Name what the branch is DOING: preventing the runners from moving forward.
That is the definition of an obstacle, word for word.
An assignment is given work, an alert is a warning, a concept is an idea — none of them block a path.

ex.main: **An obstacle.** Anything that stands between you and forward motion — physical like a branch, or invisible like fear — earns the name.
ex.tip: Obstacle questions often hide the definition in the sentence itself ('blocked', 'in the way', 'couldn't get past').

questions.q: In which sentence is 'patient' used as a NOUN?
opts: The patient line of customers stretched out the door.
Grandpa is patient with my hundred questions.
The nurse brought the patient an extra blanket.
Be patient — the cookies need ten more minutes.
questions.hint: The noun version is a person in a doctor's care.
steps: Patient the adjective describes someone willing to wait; patient the noun IS someone — a person under medical care.
Test each: 'patient line' describes the line, 'is patient' and 'be patient' describe people's behavior — all adjectives.
'Brought the patient a blanket' — the patient is a person receiving care. Noun.

ex.main: **The nurse's patient.** When 'patient' has a nurse or doctor nearby and names a person, it is the noun.
ex.tip: Same trick as alert: describing, doing, or naming? Naming a person or thing = noun.

questions.q: The new crossing signal gives ___ six extra seconds to reach the other side.
steps: Who uses a crossing signal? People traveling on foot.
Pedestrian means exactly that — ped- is the foot root, like in pedal.
Patients belong in a clinic sentence; the near-lookalike is the trap.

ex.main: **Pedestrians.** Crosswalks, sidewalks and walk signals are pedestrian territory. The patients/pedestrians lookalike trap is a Wordly Wise favorite — read the whole word.
ex.tip: Roots rescue you here: ped = foot (pedal, pedestrian), pat- in patient comes from 'suffering/enduring'. Different families.

questions.q: "Feeling a cold coming on, Dad retired right after dinner." What does 'retired' mean HERE?
questions.hint: The cold and the clock are the clues.
steps: Retire has two meanings: stop working at a certain age, or go to bed.
Check the clues: a cold coming on, right after dinner — this is about one evening, not a career.
So retired here means went to bed. 'Got tired again' is a sound-alike trick — re-tired is not a word the way it looks.

ex.main: **Went to bed.** Context picks the meaning: careers end once; going to bed happens nightly. A cold after dinner points firmly at bedtime.
ex.tip: For multi-meaning words, the sentence always votes. Ask which meaning the OTHER words in the sentence support.
